blocked.name: Mole
blocking: Ají de gallina's chilli cell is factually wrong: it leads 'dried chilli' with 'ají amarillo'. Ají amarillo in ají de gallina is used fresh, frozen or as paste — the dried form is a different article, ají mirasol, and is the substitute rather than the norm. Since the lead chip of `chilli` is a fork position, this puts the dish in the wrong branch. Fix: either ['fresh chilli', 'ají amarillo paste'] (dropping ají panca, which is genuinely dried and not canonical here), or keep it dried and rename the chip 'ají mirasol (dried ají amarillo)'. Do not leave a fresh pepper filed as dried.

Check 4 fails on the `prep` facet. Three dishes describe the same move — chilli fried in fat — under three unshareable lead chips: 'chillies fried in lard' (poblano, negro, coloradito, manchamanteles), 'chilli fried in oil' (ají de gallina), 'chilli bloomed in ghee' (korma). Under the 'By first move' nesting these become three separate branches, two of them singletons, and the tree cannot fork on the move the standfirst says is decision two. Fix: give all six the same lead chip ('chillies fried in fat') and demote the fat to the second chip ('in lard' / 'in oil' / 'in ghee'). Also normalise the singular/plural — 'chilli' vs 'chillies' — across all eight prep leads. 'chillies toasted dry', 'chillies go in raw', 'chillies burned to black', 'chillies soaked without toasting' and muhammara's roasting are genuinely distinct and should stay.

Check 4 also fails on `region`, which is the lead of the 'By region' nesting. Mexico is split into four unrelated top-level branches — 'Puebla', 'Oaxaca', 'Central Mexico', 'Mexico' — so mole poblano sits alone at the top level beside Senegal instead of beside the other Mexican moles, and the reading cannot show the Mexico-versus-elsewhere split the family is about. The corpus already supports country-first two-chip cells (mother-sauce.json Pipián verde ['Mexico','Puebla','Oaxaca']; chilli-condiment.json Salsa macha ['Mexico','Veracruz']). Fix: ['Mexico','Puebla'], ['Mexico','Oaxaca'] x5, ['Mexico','Central Mexico'] x2, ['Mexico'] for adobo, and for consistency ['Spain','Catalonia'], ['Syria','Aleppo'], ['India','North India'], leaving Guatemala, Peru and Senegal as they are.

The mole verde note claims it is 'the only mole in Oaxaca where nothing meets a dry comal', but the table contradicts it: manchamanteles' prep cell is ['chillies fried in lard', 'plantain fried in lard', 'fruit simmered in the sauce'] — no comal either. The row is the thing that's wrong, not the note: manchamanteles roasts garlic, onion and tomato on the comal like its Oaxacan siblings. Fix: add 'aromatics charred on the comal' to manchamanteles' prep (which also gives it the shared second chip its siblings have), and the verde claim then stands.

Muhammara's prep chip 'peppers roasted whole' names an ingredient that appears nowhere in its chilli cell, which lists only ['dried chilli', 'Aleppo pepper'] — dried flakes, which are not roasted whole. Your own dip.json entry for the same dish says 'roasted red pepper pounded in with them'. Fix: put the roasted red pepper in the chilli cell (e.g. ['dried chilli', 'Aleppo pepper', 'roasted red pepper']) or change the prep chip to name what is actually roasted, so the row stops describing a step on an ingredient it does not contain.

The 'On the thickener' note asserts 'Romesco and mole poblano are not related; they are two solutions to one problem that happen to agree' — stated as fact, contested, and contradicted three rows earlier by the ají de gallina note, which credits that dish's bread-and-nut body to 'a Spanish bread-and-almond sauce'. Mole poblano's almonds, sesame, cinnamon, raisins, fried bread and lard are the post-conquest Spanish half of the dish, from the same picada/almond-sauce tradition romesco comes from. Fix: keep the convergence point for the genuinely independent cases (pipián, mafé) and rewrite the romesco sentence so it says contact and convergence are both in play — the ground-nut-and-bread trick travelled with the Spanish, the chillies and the comal did not.

Pipián verde contradicts its own entry in mother-sauce.json, which a reader can reach from the same site: here it is region ['Central Mexico'] with 'tomatillo simmered soft'; there it is ['Mexico','Puebla','Oaxaca'] with 'tomatillos blended in raw'. Pick one answer for both files — the raw-blended tomatillo is the one that makes the 'nothing toasted' grouping with mole verde coherent — and align the region cells.
reasons: Check 1 (uniqueness) passes cleanly. All 16 rows are distinct; no pair differs in fewer than two facets. Nearest neighbours are negro/coloradito (differ in chilli, prep, add, body) and amarillo/verde (differ in chilli, prep, add) — both real dishes, not one written twice.
Check 2 (dead columns) passes. chilli forks 2 ways at the lead chip, prep 8, add 3, body 5, region 10. Nothing is decoration.

Check 3 (compound chips) passes. The only chips containing 'and' are 'nuts and seeds' (a deliberate category label that forks against 'no nuts or seeds'), 'tomato and garlic roasted whole' and 'onion and garlic fried first' — one move applied to two aromatics, which matches settled corpus practice (114 such chips across the other families, e.g. dip.json's 'shallots and garlic charred in their skins').

Check 5 (parent) is right. No dish carries a parent, and the 'On depth' note argues correctly that the seven Oaxacan moles are siblings made in the same kitchens, not a descent line. Negro really is not coloradito-plus-burnt-seeds. Do not add arrows here.

Check 6 (parochial) passes for a family whose name is Nahuatl: 10 Mexican, 1 Guatemalan, 5 further afield (Catalonia, Aleppo, Peru, Senegal, North India). Optional expansion if you ever want a seventeenth: Georgian satsivi/bazha or Turkish circassian chicken would push the nut-and-bread-thickener thesis furthest from chilli country.

Check 7, fact-checks that came back clean: chichilo as the funeral mole with beef broth is confirmed (Atlas Obscura, 'Oaxaca's Mystical Mole of Mourning'); the amarillo herb geography is exactly right (valleys hoja santa, coast/Sierra Sur pitiona, isthmus epazote); ñora with choricero as an accepted alternative for romesco is defensible; chilhuacle negro as effectively Oaxaca-only is right. Spellings all check out — chilhuacle, pasilla oaxaqueño, chilcostle, costeño amarillo, chile guaque, chile pasa, chile cobán, bolillo, miltomate, manchamanteles.

Check 8 (standfirst) passes. It states a thesis (mōlli means sauce; four decisions; the decisions recur elsewhere) rather than praising the food, and every part of it is checkable against the table. The 'On chocolate' arithmetic also checks out — 3 of 16 take chocolate, and amarillo, verde and chichilo take none.

Non-blocking suggestions: (a) the 'By thickener' nesting is ordered body -> add -> chilli, but body cells carry 2-3 chips that exhaust the group first, so 'chilli' is almost never reached — amarillo and verde end up separated by 'miltomate vs epazote' rather than by dried-vs-fresh chilli, which is the decision that actually divides them; reordering to body -> chilli -> add would fix it. (b) Manchamanteles leads 'add' with 'fruit' although it also carries almond, so under any add-first reading it disappears from the nut branch. (c) Oaxacan mole verde usually carries white beans; a 'white bean' chip in its add cell would earn its place. (d) The bare 'yours' keywords 'adobo' and 'korma' now collide with braise.json's Filipino adobo and its own korma entry — tolerated elsewhere in the corpus (avgolemono, wonton, massaman) but worth knowing.

Sources consulted: https://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/oaxaca-mole-chichilo , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aj%C3%AD_de_gallina , https://www.196flavors.com/romesco-sauce/ , https://gudomagazine.com/mole-amarillo-en-las-8-regiones-oaxaca/

blocked.name: Vinaigrette
blocking: Tarator's fat chip 'milled from raw hulled seed' is wrong, and the goma dare note repeats it ('Levantine tahini is milled from raw seed... neri goma from seed toasted nearly to burning'). The family's own cited source, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tahini, says the hulled kernels are skimmed, toasted and ground, and that the seeds are 'more commonly roasted than raw' — untoasted product is sold separately as 'raw tahini'. The real contrast between tahini and neri goma is roast depth, not raw versus toasted. Change the chip to 'milled from lightly roasted hulled seed' and the note to something like: 'Levantine tahini is milled from lightly roasted seed and tastes green and faintly bitter, neri goma from seed roasted far darker and tastes of the toast.'

Mojo picón note: 'The same solution as salsa verde reached at the other end of the Mediterranean.' The Canary Islands are Atlantic, about 100 km off the Moroccan coast — not the Mediterranean at either end. Rewrite as 'reached again a thousand miles away in the Atlantic'. (The bread bind itself is sound: the cited culturatradicionalgc.org/mojos/ page lists 'Miga de pan' in the mojo picón ingredients and says older recipes soaked it in vinegar first — keep that.)

Sauce vierge note: 'Michel Guérard's invention and barely fifty years old' contradicts the source you cite. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sauce_vierge has Guérard popularising it in the 1980s and says that in its original form the sauce was a Mediterranean preparation — it predates him, which also kills the line that it 'reads as though it had always been there'. Guérard also cooked at Eugénie-les-Bains in the Landes, so 'Provence' and 'his invention' cannot both stand. Fix to something like 'Guérard put it on menus in the nouvelle cuisine years; the mixture itself is older and Mediterranean', and keep Provence as an idiom claim rather than an origin.

Vinaigrette note: 'A teaspoon of it puts enough emulsifier in the bowl to hold three times its volume of oil against a quarter as much vinegar.' Two problems. 'Its volume' has no referent — read as the mustard's, a teaspoon holding three teaspoons of oil is not a trick worth naming, since the standard teaspoon of Dijon carries three tablespoons of oil. And 'a quarter as much vinegar' contradicts the fat chip 'three parts to one of vinegar': at 3:1 the vinegar is a third of the oil and a quarter of the total. Restate with one referent and a ratio that matches the chip, e.g. 'a teaspoon of it will hold three tablespoons of oil against one of vinegar'.

The default reading ('By what holds it together') never reaches the fat column for the eight unbound dishes, so the page never says that ponzu, nước chấm and nam jim jaew have no fat at all — the exact point of the note 'On the fat that is not there'. Cause: grow() forks positionally on chip index, and inside the 'nothing' bucket the index-1 chips fork because Ponzu and Ponzu shoyu share 'meant to be thin'; the refinement guard cannot rescue it either, because Sauce vierge has a chip at index 2. Rendered output today is: nothing → 'left to separate on purpose — Sauce vierge' / 'chopped with a knife rather than blended — Chimichurri' / 'stirred rather than whisked — Chermoula' / 'the syrup carries its own body — Nar ekşili sos' / 'meant to be thin' → … / 'water lets it down almost to a drink — Nước chấm' / 'stirred again at the table — Yangnyeomjang'. Fix: reduce every 'nothing' bind cell to the single chip 'nothing' (move the descriptions into the dish notes, where most of them already appear) so the tree drops through to fat. Optionally also split the bucket into the honest answers the prose already gives — chermoula 'ground spice in suspension', nar ekşili sos 'the syrup's own body', nước chấm 'sugar and water' — but that alone does not fix it; the cells still have to be one chip long.

Both parent/child pairs are forked in the tree by a hedge chip rather than by the thing that makes them different dishes. Ponzu renders as '• sudachi — Ponzu' beside '• rice vinegar to steady it — Ponzu shoyu' in all three readings, because the child drops 'sudachi' and 'kabosu' from its acid cell — so the page states that ponzu is the sudachi one, which is not true and is not what the note claims ('ponzu plus soy sauce'). Give Ponzu shoyu the parent's acid and bind cells verbatim so soy in `aroma` is the only difference; also move mirin into the parent, since plain ponzu is normally made with it and leaving it only in the child adds a second undeclared difference. Same defect at the top of the page: 'red or white' is two values in one chip (check 3) and it is what separates '• red or white — Vinaigrette' from '• white — Ravigote', instead of the capers and soft herbs. Drop the hedge from the base acid cell and let the pair sit as sibling leaves.

Region grain is mixed, and 'By region' currently renders as twelve singletons with only France and Japan grouping. Provence is a top-level bucket beside France even though sauce vierge is French; Sicily and Piedmont are top-level with no Italy anywhere, so salmoriglio and salsa verde never meet. Lead every region cell at the same grain and keep the local name second: ['France','Provence'], ['Italy','Sicily','Calabria'], ['Italy','Piedmont','Lombardy'], and for consistency ['Thailand','Isan','Laos'] and ['Spain','Canary Islands'].

Chip position 1 of the `fat` cell carries four different kinds of information — a ratio ('three parts to one of vinegar'), a quality ('green and raw'), an alternative oil ('sunflower oil in as many kitchens', 'argan oil in the Souss') and a timing ('poured into the mortar last') — and because the tree forks on position, 'By the fat' now files chermoula as 'olive oil → argan oil in the Souss' and chimichurri as 'olive oil → sunflower oil in as many kitchens', i.e. under a branch of the oil they are being distinguished for not using. Standardise position 1 on one kind of qualifier (the quality chip) and push alternatives and ratios to the end of the cell.
reasons: File reviewed: /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/data/canon/vinaigrette.json (16 dishes, 5 facets, 3 nestings). I ported grow() from /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/lib/canon.ts and rendered all three readings, so the structural findings are what the page will actually draw.
Check 1 passes: no two rows are identical; all 16 differ in at least one chip.
Check 2 passes: no decorative column. bind splits six ways, fat four, acid six, aroma is unique per dish and does real work as the third level of 'By the fat'.

Check 5 passes: both parents are real (ravigote is vinaigrette plus capers and soft herbs; ponzu shoyu is ponzu plus soy) and nothing else is parented on mere resemblance. The 'On depth' note defends that correctly for the sesame pair and the bread pair.

Check 6 passes: eight Europe/Mediterranean, one South America, three MENA/Levant, five East and Southeast Asia. Not one continent in a global costume. Worth noting anyway: three entries from Japan and one from Korea but nothing from China, where a liangban dressing (light soy, Chinkiang vinegar, sesame oil, chilli oil, sugar) is the obvious sibling of yangnyeomjang; and a Senegalese yassa marinade (onion, lemon, oil, mustard) would be the only sub-Saharan entry. Both optional.
Check 8 passes: the standfirst names four decisions, matches four facets, and every clause in it is a checkable claim rather than praise.

Non-blocking, cross-family: data/canon/dip.json already carries a dish called 'Tahini sauce' (Levant, sesame paste, lemon, seizes on contact) which is this family's Tarator, and both files claim the search term 'tahini sauce' in `yours`. Suggest dropping 'tahini sauce' from this family's `yours` and adding 'taratour' (the note already gives that spelling).

Non-blocking: `yours` claims 'salsa verde', which will catch everyone who means the Mexican tomatillo salsa. The family disambiguates hot ravigote, Bulgarian tarator and mojo verde but not this one; one line in the salsa verde note would close it.

Non-blocking: the Tarator note says the Bulgarian tarator is 'a cold cucumber soup and unrelated', which skips the Turkish/Balkan tarator that the Bulgarian soup is actually named after — walnut or hazelnut pounded with bread, garlic and vinegar, i.e. a third instance of the bread bind sitting under the same name. Either widen the disambiguation or add it as a dish.

Non-blocking: the cited Ravigote source has the hot version built on 'a vegetable or meat broth, or a velouté', not strictly a velouté; and the canonical cold version lists chives among the herbs and 'shallots or onion'. Two-word fixes if you want them.

blocked.name: Compound butter
blocking: Gentleman's Relish: the maturation is invented. Drop the prep chip 'matured in the pot' (the sourced facts are anchovy min 60%, butter, rusk and a secret spice mix, John Osborn 1828 — no source describes ageing in the jar), and cut 'and time under the lid' from the dish note. The chip could become 'rusk beaten in' or simply leave prep as raw + pounded to a paste.

The 'On depth' note overclaims: 'both because a written recipe says so' is true only for Colbert. Gentleman's Relish's formula is a trade secret, so no written recipe states it as anchovy butter plus spices plus 'a month in the pot'. Rewrite so Colbert is the arithmetic case and Gentleman's Relish is read as an anchovy butter from what is in the jar, not from a recipe.

Harissa butter's region 'Tunisia' labels the paste, not the butter. Everywhere else in that column region means where the dish comes from (Burgundy, Geneva, Brittany, Japan, United States); harissa butter is a modern Western compound butter built on a Tunisian paste — recipe sites label the same thing 'Moroccan' — and Tunisian cooking is olive-oil based, so a Tunisia branch in the 'By region' tree containing only a restaurant invention asserts something false. Either relabel it (e.g. 'modern', or Tunisia via France) or replace it with a chilli butter that has a real regional home.

Niter kibbeh is Eritrean as well as Ethiopian (tesmi in Tigrinya, per the cited Wikipedia source). The region facet accepts multiple chips elsewhere in the corpus (dough-with-filling uses ['Tibet','Nepal']) — add 'Eritrea'.

The region column names the same country two ways: Gentleman's Relish is 'England' and bone marrow butter is 'Britain'. Pick one (England for both is the tighter reading — Elsenham for the relish, London marrow-and-parsley for the butter).

The 'Butter that keeps' note opposes clarifying and salting as either/or, but smen is both: the standard method boils, skims and strains the butter before the salt goes in and the pot is sealed. Reword so the contrast is what does the preserving (milk solids removed vs lactic fermentation under salt) rather than implying smen is unclarified.

Beurre Colbert's prep chip says 'veal glaze beaten in' while its own note and Escoffier say melted meat glaze (glace de viande). Make the chip read 'meat glaze beaten in' so chip, note and source agree.
reasons: Structure is sound. No two dishes share a row (checked all 16 signatures across the 5 facets), and no pair even differs in fewer than 2 chips — so nothing is one dish written twice.

No dimension is decoration: aromatic, prep, form, use and region all vary. prep splits raw x10 / roasted first x2 / blanched / steeped / simmered / salted; form splits chilled log x6, soft x5, potted x2, set hard, frozen hard, clarified; use splits melted on x6, spread cold x5, cooked with x2, baked in, sealed inside, stirred into.

No chip is two moves joined. The two 'and' chips ('melted and strained', 'sealed and aged') read as single moves phrased naturally, matching corpus convention elsewhere (chilli-condiment: 'the two married and aged in open crocks'; vinaigrette: 'whisked until it turns pale and thick').

Multi-chip cells lead with the shared move, so all three nestings fork cleanly. Leaf collisions occur only where they should — maitre d'hotel with its child Colbert, anchovy butter with its child Gentleman's Relish, and miso/harissa as genuine siblings that still differ in form and region.

parent is used twice and both are real descents in kind: Colbert is verifiably maitre d'hotel butter plus tarragon and pale meat glaze (Escoffier, 141), and Gentleman's Relish is an anchovy-and-butter paste. No descent is missing — Kyiv and snail butter are correctly siblings, not a line.
Standfirst is a claim, not praise: it names the three working dimensions (what goes in, raw vs cooked first, what the butter is asked to do) and the count of sixteen is correct.

Coverage is defensible rather than parochial — Europe holds 11 of 16 and France or francophone Switzerland 8 of those, but 'compound butter' is a French codification and the family reaches Japan, Ethiopia, Morocco, Ukraine and the US. If anything is added later, add it outside Europe (Levantine samneh, or a Southeast Asian garlic butter for grilled shellfish) rather than a ninth French one.

Non-blocking observations: (a) the aromatic column mixes levels in its lead chip — categories (herb, spice, fermented paste, shellfish, seaweed) beside ingredients (garlic, anchovy, bone marrow, salt, honey) — so 'By what goes in' forks into ten branches of two different kinds, and a reader will notice snail and Kyiv butter sitting outside the herb branch though both are herb butters; (b) Cafe de Paris under an 'anchovy' lead is a strain, since its identity is the twenty-item blend, not the anchovy; (c) form is never used as a nesting axis (the corpus allows that — dough-with-filling never nests on filling) but it is this family's sharpest split, and a 'By form' nesting would earn its keep; (d) beurre de homard's 'roasted first' is modern practice — Escoffier pounds the shells and coral of an already-cooked lobster — and 'the aromatic is thrown away' sits awkwardly beside 'coral' as a chip, since in the pounded-and-sieved version the coral goes through; (e) smen's 'wild oregano' is a fair reading of Moroccan zaatar, but the cited Wikipedia source names thyme and roasted fenugreek if you want to be source-tight.

blocked.name: Salted and preserved fish
blocking: FACT — Hákarl note is wrong about why the shark is loaded with urea. It carries urea and TMAO to stay in osmotic balance with seawater (TMAO counteracts urea's destabilising effect on proteins, and both double as antifreeze); buoyancy in sharks comes from the oil-rich liver, not from osmolytes. Replace 'instead of salt to stay buoyant' with something like 'instead of salt, to stay in balance with the sea it swims in'. The toxicity mechanism as written is fine (TMAO breaking down to trimethylamine).

FACT — Colatura's note asserts more than the record supports, and contradicts the family's own data. 'Rome's garum by unbroken descent — the Amalfi coast simply never stopped' skips the gap between antiquity and the 13th-century Cistercians at Cetara who are the first documented link, and it is contradicted two rows up in this very table: garum is 'guts left in', while these anchovies have 'heads pulled off by hand' and no viscera — which is exactly the technical break historians point to (no gut enzymes, lower protein, higher salinity). It also sits badly against the 'On depth' note, which says garum is not colatura's parent. Reword to claim the same liquid rather than an unbroken line, e.g. 'Rome tapped the same liquid off the same coast — though with the guts left in, which is not what happens here. Whether the line ever actually broke is a story Cetara tells better than the record does.'

STRUCTURE — Reading 2, 'By food or seasoning', collapses. Because chip 1 of every `end` cell is a per-dish serving detail, 'eaten as food' forks into nine singleton leaves labelled 'soaked three days first', 'cooked before eating', 'torn into strips', and `preserve` and `fish` are never consumed; 'used as seasoning' forks into six. The reading the standfirst advertises therefore never shows how anything was preserved. Fix by making chip 1 of `end` shared vocabulary and pushing the serving detail to chip 2 (or into the note): for food, 'soaked back first' (Bacalhau, Tørrfisk, Acciughe) / 'cooked first' (Kippers, Surume) / 'eaten as it is' (Surströmming, Hákarl, Jeotgal, Shiokara); for seasoning, 'a spoonful of liquid' (Colatura, Garum, Nước mắm) / 'grated or pounded to a dust' (Bottarga, Katsuobushi, Maldive fish) / 'a lump dropped in the pot' (Guedj). That lets the fork fall on preserve underneath.

STRUCTURE — Three `end` cells claim both sides of the axis the family is built on, and one of them loses a dish the notes explicitly count. Acciughe ends '...and melted into sauces as seasoning', Bottarga '...or sliced thin and eaten as food', Jeotgal '...and drained off as aekjeot for kimchi' — each a second thing bolted onto a chip with 'and'/'or' (check 3). Jeotgal is the real problem: 'On food and seasoning' lists aekjeot alongside garum, colatura, nước mắm and guedj as seasoning that went all the way, yet in the data it is a trailing chip inside an 'eaten as food' cell, so aekjeot never appears under 'used as seasoning' anywhere. This is the identical move to colatura — solids eaten, liquid drawn off — so treat it identically: add a dish 'Aekjeot' with `parent: "Jeotgal"`, `end: ["used as seasoning", ...]`, and drop the trailing chip from Jeotgal. Drop the other two trailing chips too, or promote them the same way.

STRUCTURE — The fermented branch forks on inconsistent vocabulary, so two dishes making the same decision render as two separate one-dish branches. Chip 2 answers 'how much salt' for Garum / Nước mắm / Jeotgal ('salt heavy enough to stop rot') and Hákarl ('no salt at all'), but Surströmming says 'brine too weak to stop it' and Shiokara 'salt too light to keep it long' — the same answer twice, so they never group — while Guedj's 'left open to the air first' answers a different question entirely (order, not quantity). Give Surströmming and Shiokara one shared chip ('salt too weak to stop it') and let them fork on chip 3 ('left open in the barrel' vs 'its own liver stirred back in'); give Guedj a salt-level chip at position 2 and move 'salt only after it has started' to position 3, where its genuinely distinctive reversal belongs.

STRUCTURE — The `region` facet mixes country and sub-place in the leading slot, which splits Italy in reading 3. Bottarga leads with 'Sardinia', so it renders as a peer of the 'Italy' node holding Acciughe and Colatura; make it ["Italy", "Sardinia"]. Garum's 'Roman Mediterranean' is fine as a deliberate exception, but Acciughe's second chip is 'Spain' — a co-country sitting in the sub-place slot, which would render as 'Italy > Spain > Acciughe sotto sale' the moment anything else joined that branch. Either use ["Italy", "Liguria"] and put the Cantabrian anchovy in the note, or split Spain out as its own dish.

COVERAGE — Parochial for a family named 'Salted and preserved fish'. Nine of sixteen dishes are European, and the entire salted branch — Bacalhau, Acciughe, Colatura, Bottarga — is Western European, as if salting fish were a Mediterranean-and-Atlantic idea. Nothing from China, South Asia, the Americas, or the Middle East; and the seasoning argument, which is the family's best idea, omits the largest body of preserved-fish seasoning on earth. I checked the rest of the corpus: belacan, terasi and prahok appear in data/canon/curry-paste.json and braise.json only as ingredients, so they are covered nowhere as dishes. Add at least (a) one non-European salt-dried fish — Chinese 咸鱼 salt fish, Bengali shutki or Tamil karuvadu, Filipino daing/tuyo — so the salted fork is not a European column, and (b) one of the paste/rice-ferment line — belacan/terasi/kapi, or prahok/pla ra/padaek, or funazushi — which introduces a fifth preserving move (rice or grain feeding the ferment) the family currently has no example of. Fesikh (Egypt) or Pacific Northwest smoke-dried salmon would close the Middle East and Americas gaps if you want more than two.
reasons: Checks 1 and 2 pass cleanly. No two dishes share a row — I diffed all 16 signatures, and in fact the `preserve` column alone separates every dish in the family. Every dimension carries varying values; none is decoration.

The four-technique spine (salted / dried / fermented / smoked) is real and consistently worded, and the notes are unusually good — 'On what actually preserves' correctly demotes smoke to a surface treatment, and 'On depth' correctly refuses to make garum the parent of colatura. `parent` is used exactly once, where it is genuinely 'the same barrel plus one move'.

The standfirst makes a claim rather than praising the food, and names the axis the family turns on (dinner vs the thing you season dinner with). One quibble: 'Smoke seals the surface' contradicts the family's own note, which says smoke 'dries the surface and lays down phenols' and 'on its own buys days'. Consider 'Smoke dries the surface and coats it in phenols.'

Evidence for the nesting problems below: I extracted `grow()` from /Users/dmarzari/Server-Sites/Cookbook/src/lib/canon.ts and rendered all three readings. Reading 1 works. Reading 2 ('By food or seasoning') renders 'eaten as food' as nine flat leaves — 'soaked three days first — Bacalhau', 'torn into strips — Surume' — and never reaches `preserve` or `fish` at all. Reading 3 puts 'Sardinia' beside 'Italy' as a peer.

Softer flags, not blocking: 'tiny shrimp or anchovy' (Jeotgal) and 'catfish or capitaine' (Guedj) are two things in one chip (check 3); Katsuobushi's mould step is a fermentation filed under 'smoked' — defensible, since the smoke does the drying, but the notes never say so; 'the cheapest preserved seafood in Asia' (Surume) is an unverifiable superlative; 'boiled in its own brine' (Maldive fish) is really boiled in salted water; and in reading 1 the acciughe/colatura pair walks a seven-level spine in which the preserve chip 'ripened a year' is immediately restated by the keep chip 'a year in the barrel' — trim one.
